extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners prosecuting design patent applications
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural and substantive examination standards from MPEP §1504 for evaluating whether claimed designs meet statutory requirements (35 U.S.C. 171), with special guidance for computer-generated images, ornamentality, drawings, titles/claims, multiple-part designs, and related formal actions (e.g., Quayle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary statement of rejection format
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim stands rejected under [1].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as summary statement of rejection(s) in Office action. In bracket 1, insert appropriate basis for rejection, i.e., statutory provisions, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ex parte Quayle - claimed design patentable but formal matters remain
rubrics_metrics.description: This application is in condition for allowance except for the following formal matters: [1]. Prosecution on the merits is closed in accordance with practice under Ex parte Quayle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when examiner determines the claim is patentable under all statutory requirements but formal matters need to be addressed prior to allowance. Set a shortened two-month statutory period for reply (extensions under 37 CFR 1.136 possible but reply cannot exceed six months). If, after a reply, a rejection should be given, withdraw indication of allowability and reopen prosecution using the specified form paragraph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation to employ a patent attorney or agent (design applications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant might consider it desirable to employ the services of a registered patent attorney or agent; the USPTO cannot aid in selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In pro se design applications, notify applicant in the first Office action that employing a registered patent practitioner may be desirable. Provide copy of 'Guide To Filing A Design Patent Application' where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation to employ a professional patent draftsperson (design drawings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant might consider employing the services of a professional patent draftsperson familiar with design practice because the value of a design patent depends largely on skillful preparation of drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO cannot aid in selection. Use form paragraph where appropriate to advise applicant; list of registered attorneys/agents available at OEDCI.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory basis under 35 U.S.C. 171
rubrics_metrics.description: Whoever invents any new, original, and ornamental design for an article of manufacture may obtain a patent therefor; provisions of this title relating to patents for inventions apply to patents for designs; filing date is date the specification per section 112 and required drawings are filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation includes at least three kinds of designs: (A) design for an ornament/impression/print applied to an article (surface indicia); (B) design for the shape/configuration; (C) combination of the two. Use statutory text and case law to assess subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design must be embodied in an article of manufacture (picture alone not patentable)
rubrics_metrics.description: A picture standing alone is not patentable under 35 U.S.C. 171; the design must be shown as applied to or embodied in an article of manufacture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim to a picture, print, impression, etc., per se that is not applied to or embodied in an article of manufacture should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 171 as directed to nonstatutory subject matter. Use applicable form paragraphs (e.g., ¶15.09).

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual characteristics define the design
rubrics_metrics.description: The design for an article consists of the visual characteristics or aspect displayed by the article — the appearance presented by the article creating an impression on the observer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this concept when analyzing what the claimed design covers; design subject matter may relate to configuration/shape, surface ornamentation, or both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design inseparable from article; must be definite and reproducible
rubrics_metrics.description: Design is inseparable from the article to which it is applied and cannot exist alone merely as a scheme of ornamentation; it must be a definite preconceived thing, capable of reproduction, not merely the chance result of functional combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure compliance with 35 U.S.C. 171 and 35 U.S.C. 112 (written description); see case law (e.g., Blisscraft). Use form paragraphs for subsequent actions as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer-generated electronic images must meet article-of-manufacture requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Design applications for computer-generated electronic images must comply with the article of manufacture requirement of 35 U.S.C. 171.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the complete-disclosure review and follow the specific procedures in subsection I (review title/claim, specification, drawings) to determine whether the design is embodied in an article of manufacture (e.g., a display panel).

rubrics_metrics.name: General principle — mere display on screen insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere display of a picture on a screen is not significantly different from display on paper and is not enough to convert a picture into a design for an article of manufacture (Ex parte Strijland).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Images merely displayed on display panels are not eligible under 35 U.S.C. 171 unless the image is more than a displayed picture (e.g., a computer icon or GUI that is integral/active component of computer operation and embodied in a programmed computer/display panel).

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer icons and GUIs eligible only as embodied in an article
rubrics_metrics.description: A computer icon or GUI is considered more than a mere display and can be eligible under 35 U.S.C. 171 if properly presented and claimed (e.g., drawing fully discloses the design as embodied in the article of manufacture such as a display panel).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims/titles should be to an article of manufacture (e.g., 'display panel with computer icon'); icon/GUI alone should not be claimed. Ensure the drawing and description disclose the icon/GUI embodied in a display panel (solid or broken lines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Title and claim must adequately designate an article of manufacture
rubrics_metrics.description: Review title and claim language to determine whether they describe a design for an article of manufacture under 35 U.S.C. 171; titles/claims should not be for an icon or GUI alone but for an article (e.g., 'computer screen with an icon').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Object under 37 CFR 1.153(a) or 1.1067(a) when title/claim fail to designate a particular article. Examples of inadequate titles/claims: 'display screen with virtual image', 'virtual image for display on computer screen', 'computer icon'. Examples of adequate titles/claims: 'computer screen with an icon', 'display panel with GUI', 'portion of a computer screen with an icon'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must contain characteristic feature statement when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Review the specification to determine whether a characteristic feature statement is present and whether it describes the claimed subject matter as a computer icon or GUI embodied in a display panel or portion thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A descriptive (characteristic feature) statement can narrow claim scope (see McGrady v. Aspenglas). Use it to determine proper claim scope and support for amendments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings must show the article (display panel) in sufficient views
rubrics_metrics.description: Review the drawing to determine whether a display panel, or a portion thereof, is shown in sufficient views to fully disclose the design as embodied in the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If drawing does not depict the icon/GUI embodied in a display panel (solid or broken lines), reject under 35 U.S.C. 171. If disclosure as a whole suggests embodiment, indicate drawing may be amended to overcome rejection; warn that adding new matter will not be allowed and may render claim subject to 35 U.S.C. 112(a) rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure on applicant reply for computer-generated image rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon applicant reply: enter any appropriate amendments and review all arguments and the entire record, including amendments, to determine whether the drawing, title, and specification clearly disclose the icon or GUI embodied in a display panel or portion thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If by a preponderance of the evidence applicant has established embodiment in a display panel, withdraw the rejection under 35 U.S.C. 171. Apply preponderance standard per In re Oetiker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples illustrating acceptable and unacceptable presentations
rubrics_metrics.description: Provided examples (e.g., 'Computer display screen with icon' — acceptable; 'Virtual paper stack' — not acceptable) show when claims/titles/drawings comply with 35 U.S.C. 171 or should be objected/rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples to guide objections and rejections; where possible suggest replacement figures or amendments supported by original disclosure. Note examples of acceptable and unacceptable claim language and titles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of type fonts in design claims
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO personnel should not reject claims for type fonts under 35 U.S.C. 171 on the basis that modern computer-generation methods do not require solid printing blocks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize historical granting of design patents to type fonts; do not apply article-of-manufacture rejections merely because fonts are computer-generated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changeable (animated) computer-generated images — descriptive statement required
rubrics_metrics.description: Animated or changeable images may be the subject of a design claim shown in two or more views. A descriptive statement must be included describing the transitional nature and making clear that the process/period of transition forms no part of the claimed design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide sample descriptive statements (e.g., 'The appearance of the image sequentially transitions between the images shown in Figs. 1-8. The process or period in which one image transitions to another image forms no part of the claimed design.'). Object to title/claim if they fail to designate a particular article (37 CFR 1.153/1.1067) and suggest amending to 'computer display screen with an animated icon.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Design comprising multiple articles or multiple parts
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed design may encompass multiple articles or multiple parts within a single article, but the title must identify a single entity of manufacture made up by the parts (e.g., set, pair, combination, unit, assembly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a descriptive statement in the specification clarifying that the claim is directed to the collective appearance. If separate parts are shown in a single view, embrace parts by a bracket '}'. For multiple parts of a single article, show article in broken lines and parts in solid lines (no bracket needed). See MPEP §1503.01.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornamentality vs. functionality — primary ornamentality requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: To be patentable, a design must be 'primarily ornamental.' In determining whether a design is primarily functional or ornamental, view the claimed design in its entirety; the ultimate question is the overall appearance, not the function or decoration of separate features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider that ornamentality must be created for the purpose of ornamenting (In re Carletti). The determination is qualitative based on ornamental contribution to the design as a whole, not quantitative based on feature size. Distinguish functionality of the article from functionality of the particular design of such article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie evidentiary basis required for rejection under 35 U.S.C. 171 (lack of ornamentality)
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner must make a prima facie showing that the claimed design lacks ornamentality and provide sufficient evidentiary basis for factual assumptions relied upon in such showing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper evidentiary bases include the appearance of the design itself, examiner's knowledge of the art, replies to inquiries, brochures emphasizing functional/mechanical features, specification of an analogous utility patent, or information in the application. Rejections must be supported by evidence; do not make rejections absent such evidence (see In re Jung, In re Oetiker).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific acceptable evidentiary sources for lack-of-ornamentality rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of proper evidentiary basis: (A) common knowledge in the art; (B) the appearance of the design itself; (C) the specification of a related utility patent; (D) information provided in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these to support a prima facie rejection under 35 U.S.C. 171. For mechanical articles, support functional-dictation analysis with utility patents or other sources describing the function. For general-use articles (e.g., clip), provide detailed and specific analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of lack-of-ornamentality rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Two categories: (A) a design visible in its ultimate end use which is primarily functional based on record evidence; (B) a design not visible in its normal and intended use as evidence its appearance is not a matter of concern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a proper prima facie case is made, the burden shifts to applicant to rebut. Use form paragraphs 15.08 or 15.08.01 where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant rebuttal burden and acceptable rebuttal evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Once examiner establishes a proper prima facie case of lack of ornamentality, the burden of coming forward with evidence or argument shifts to the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant may overcome rejection by providing evidence (e.g., inventor or company representative testimony) that the design was intended for the purpose of ornamenting. Attorney argument alone is insufficient; applicant should provide factual evidence. Cite Ex parte Webb and In re Carletti for guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objections under Rules of Practice (drawing/title/spec compliance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicate all objections to the disclosure for failure to comply with requirements of the Rules of Practice in Patent Cases (e.g., 37 CFR 1.71, 1.81-1.85, 1.152-1.154).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggest amendments to bring disclosure into compliance. Maintain objections to title and claim under 37 CFR 1.153(a) or 1.1067(a) until appropriately amended. Warn that amendment introducing new matter is not permitted.
